If you come from agency finance and you sit in front of a board from another industry, there is one thing you have to disarm in the first minute, and it is billings. In our world billings is the total value invoiced to clients, and it can be six or seven times revenue, because most of what we invoice is media that passes straight through us. To a board that has never worked in this industry, a billings number sounds like the size of the company, and if you let that misunderstanding stand you will spend the rest of the meeting correcting it. So say it once, plainly. Billings were four hundred million, revenue was fifty five, and the number that matters for this conversation is the fifty five. Then move on. The same applies to pacing, which everybody in advertising says twenty times a day and nobody outside it understands. If a word only exists inside your industry, define it in six words the first time you use it and never define it again.

Two thousand nineteen is the year I always get asked about, so let me take it properly. We went into it with a gross margin of about thirty one per cent, which for that mix was thin, and an overhead base built for a group that had been twice the size two years earlier. In February we lost our largest account. I remember telling the board that we would not chase revenue to replace it, and I remember the silence afterwards. We tried cutting discretionary spend first, which bought us almost nothing, so we stopped doing that and went at the overhead itself. By the fourth quarter the margin was thirty four and a half, on a smaller top line. The thing I would underscore is that we never wrote off a receivable that year, which in a year like that is the number I am actually proud of.
